strengths: Clean and controlled experimental formulation: The paper designs a minimal, synthetic 1D image-text setup that cleanly isolates the problem of relational learning and compositional generalization (single-object, seen-pair configuration, and unseen-pair generalization) without confounding visual or linguistic noise.

Rigor in mechanistic decomposition: The decomposition of pre-softmax attention logits into embedding-embedding (EE), embedding-position (EP), position-embedding (PE), and position-position (PP) terms provides a crystal-clear explanation of how attention asymmetry emerges.

Comprehensive ablation and theoretical validation: The authors thoroughly validate their hypothesis through systematic zeroing of the EP/BP terms (showing drops to chance 0.5 on relational discrimination while preserving pair recognition), accompanied by an insightful analytical derivation in Appendix I showing why the condition |Π| > |T| is mathematically necessary for out-of-distribution pair generalization.

Extension to modern architectures: The paper extends beyond simple learnable absolute positional embeddings to Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), uncovering two distinct mechanisms (bias-induced gradient and low-rank subspace alignment) that enable symmetry breaking.
weaknesses: Simplicity of the synthetic domain: The 1D discrete grid with single-pixel object identities is far removed from continuous, multi-patch 2D ViTs and natural captions. While appropriate for mechanistic reverse-engineering, whether these precise gradient dynamics transfer to standard 2D ViT/CLIP checkpoints pre-trained on web-scale data remains an open question.

Limited depth on multi-layer inter-head dynamics: The primary mechanistic analysis is centered on 1-layer models without LayerNorm/MLP. Although 2-layer dynamics and head pruning are briefly touched upon in Appendices K and L, the synthesis of how multi-layer representations interact to route relational information through the network is left largely as future work.

strengths: Clear, controllable, and well-motivated experimental setup: The paper establishes a minimal 1D synthetic testbed that cleanly isolates the problem of relational spatial learning (left-right ordering) in contrastive vision-language models without the confounding factors of naturalistic clutter.

Rigorously executed mechanistic decomposition: Expanding the pre-softmax attention logits into EE, EP, PE, and PP terms provides a crisp, quantitative explanation for left-right symmetry breaking, demonstrating convincingly that the cross-interaction between token and positional embeddings (EW_QK P^T) induces the required spatial gradient.

Comprehensive ablation and causal validation: The authors validate their hypotheses through targeted zeroing ablations of logit components, demonstrating that ablating the EP term reduces unseen-pair relation discrimination to chance (~0.5) while preserving pair identity recognition.

Deep extension to RoPE and multi-head dynamics: The mathematical and empirical treatment of Rotary Position Embeddings (App. I)—identifying both bias-induced gradients and low-rank subspace alignment—adds substantial technical depth beyond standard absolute positional embeddings.
weaknesses: Ecological validity and gap to real-world 2D VLMs: The findings are derived entirely on an idealized 1D synthetic testbed with single-pixel objects and rigid caption templates. While acknowledged in the discussion, the paper lacks validation or probing on standard pre-trained 2D CLIP models (e.g., ViT-B/32 on Winoground/ARO), leaving open whether real-world models rely on analogous attention gradient mechanisms.

Limited depth on multi-layer interactions: The mechanistic decomposition requires simplifying the vision encoder to a single layer without LayerNorm or MLP. Although Appendix L shows suggestive gradient patterns in a 2-layer model, a full mechanistic account of how these spatial gradients propagate and compose across deeper layers remains largely unaddressed.

Incomplete explanation of text encoder representations with dual relations: When both 'left' and 'right' descriptions are introduced (Section 7), the 1-layer text encoder fails and requires a 2-layer architecture, but the exact mechanism by which the 2-layer text encoder resolves relational ambiguity is not analyzed.

strengths: The paper provides a clean, principled, and controlled mechanistic interpretability framework addressing a recognized challenge in multimodal models: understanding how Transformer-based contrastive vision-language models can learn relative spatial relations.

The attention logit decomposition is technically rigorous and insightful. The authors clearly dissect pre-softmax attention into token-token, token-position, position-token, and position-position interactions, isolating the cross-term (EW_{QK}P^T) as the primary driver of horizontal attention gradients that break spatial symmetry.

The causal interventions (zeroing positional logit components at test time) convincingly demonstrate the role of this term: relational discrimination collapses to chance (~50%) while the model's ability to detect co-occurring object pairs remains intact.

The mathematical derivations and experiments in the appendix—especially regarding Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), showing how bias terms and low-rank subspace projection enable spatial asymmetry without learnable absolute position embeddings—add substantial theoretical depth to the empirical findings.
weaknesses: The experimental setting is heavily restricted to a synthetic 1D toy environment (length 10, single-pixel objects, templated text). While toy setups are established tools in mechanistic interpretability, the paper does not bridge these findings to 2D image patches, natural images, or pretrained models (such as CLIP ViT-B/16), leaving open whether real-world VLMs use similar mechanisms or why they consistently fail at spatial relational reasoning.

The primary mechanistic story relies on an ablated 1-layer Transformer block stripped of LayerNorm and MLPs. While this simplification aids clean mathematical tractability, multi-layer architectures with non-linear MLPs and LayerNorm can distribute spatial representations across layers and channels through very different computational paths.

The experimental evaluations lack reported error bars or confidence intervals across multiple random seeds, which is particularly relevant given the observed phase transitions and training dynamics reminiscent of grokking.

strengths: Clear and rigorous mechanistic framing: The paper addresses a well-documented failure mode in vision-language models (relational and spatial reasoning) by designing a minimal, fully controllable setting to isolate when and how relational competence emerges.

Precise mathematical and causal decomposition: Decomposing pre-softmax attention logits into query-key component interactions (EE, EP, PE, PP) allows the authors to identify the specific cross-term (token-to-position embedding, EP) driving the horizontal attention gradient.

Targeted causal interventions: The inference-time ablation of specific logit components provides convincing causal evidence: ablating the EP term drops left–right discrimination to chance while preserving object identity retrieval.

Extensive supplementary validation: The authors anticipate several key criticisms and address them thoroughly in the appendices, including theoretical analyses of out-of-distribution consistency conditions, extensions to Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), 2D grid scenes, 3-object configurations, and autoregressive decoder formulations.
weaknesses: Substantial domain gap to real-world VLMs: The entire study is conducted on highly stylized synthetic setups (1D token sequences and 4x4 discrete grids) with single-token integer object identities. While common in mechanistic interpretability, the paper does not validate whether this symmetry-breaking mechanism actually operates in large-scale pre-trained CLIP models or natural image-text distributions.

Incomplete mechanistic explanation for multi-layer / bidirectional language encoders: When moving to natural bidirectional descriptions ('X is left of Y' and 'Y is right of X'), a 1-layer text encoder fails completely. While adding a second layer restores performance, the internal mechanism of the 2-layer text encoder is left largely uncharacterized due to analytical complexity.

Heavy reliance on regularization and grokking-like dynamics: Generalization in this setup is strongly dependent on high weight decay (e.g., w = 0.2) and extended training (10,000 epochs) to avoid memorization, raising questions about whether standard web-scale pre-training regimes develop similar mechanisms.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely foundational question: how vision-language encoders acquire relative spatial understanding under contrastive training, framed through a clear and principled mechanistic interpretability lens.

The pre-softmax logit decomposition into token, position, and cross terms ($E W_{QK} E^T$, $E W_{QK} P^T$, etc.) provides a precise and transparent account of how attention gradients break left-right symmetry in the vision encoder.

Causal interventions (ablation experiments) cleanly isolate the role of positional-embedding cross terms: removing the $E W_{QK} P^T$ and bias terms reduces directional discrimination to chance (~50%) while keeping object identity recognition intact.

The paper includes extensive extensions that substantially broaden the scope beyond the basic 1D setup: theoretical and empirical analysis of Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), extension to 2D grid inputs, extension to 3-object scenes, an autoregressive VLM testbed, and an approximate decomposition incorporating LayerNorm.
weaknesses: The empirical findings are established purely within simplified synthetic environments (1D sequences and 4x4 toy images with integer tokens). While appropriate for a mechanistic study, the gap to real-world CLIP ViTs trained on natural photographic images with continuous visual features remains significant.

The paper notes that in the bidirectional captioning setup ('left of' and 'right of' coexisting), a 1-layer text encoder fails and requires 2 layers. However, the mechanistic operation of the 2-layer text encoder is left uncharacterized due to the complexity of multi-layer attention dynamics.

The connection to empirical failure modes in large-scale VLMs (e.g., ARO, Winoground) is primarily conceptual; the work does not provide evidence whether large-scale models fail due to the absence of these attention gradients or due to other bottlenecks (e.g., language priors or pooling).

strengths: Clear mechanistic interpretation: The decomposition of pre-softmax attention logits into token–token, token–position, position–token, and position–position components cleanly isolates the precise mechanism (specifically the horizontal attention gradient in the $E W_{QK} P^T$ cross-term) responsible for left–right symmetry breaking.

Rigorous causal interventions: The paper does not stop at correlational attention visualizations; it performs targeted ablation of specific logit terms at inference time, showing that zeroing the positional cross-term reduces spatial discrimination to random chance while preserving the model's ability to identify which objects are present.

Important empirical finding on generalization drivers: The finding that label diversity—rather than layout/positional diversity—is the primary driver of out-of-distribution relational generalization offers useful conceptual insights into how contrastive training encourages modular/relational representations.

Thorough theoretical and empirical extensions in the appendix: The manuscript provides substantial supplementary investigations, including formal conditions for OOD consistency, analyses extending to Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), extensions to 2D image grids and 3-object scenes, comparisons with autoregressive decoders, and an approximate decomposition under LayerNorm.
weaknesses: Gap between synthetic testbeds and realistic vision-language models: The core experiments rely on 1D sequences (and 4x4 2D grids) with discrete integer tokens representing single-pixel objects and template language. While appropriate for mechanistic reverse-engineering, it remains unverified whether full-scale pretrained CLIP models (e.g., OpenAI ViT-B/16) implement spatial discrimination via an identical attention gradient mechanism.

Limited complexity of spatial relations: The primary focus is strictly on binary 1D horizontal relations ('left of' / 'right of'). Although 3-object scenes and 2D grids are tested in the appendix, broader spatial semantics (such as metric distance, vertical alignment, topological containment, or 3D perspective) are not explored.

Heuristic nature of the LayerNorm decomposition: The mechanistic analysis is cleanest in the attention-only, single-layer linear regime. The proposed LayerNorm decomposition in Appendix R is an approximation due to the coupling in $\text{std}(E + P)$, leaving the full dynamics of deeper, non-linear stacks partially unresolved.
